Our approach to self-supervised image representation learning, called Deep
Optimal Transport, focuses on capturing key invariants within an image by
relating nearby visual elements through both position and orientation. By
capturing these local connections, we define a distance metric based on the
Sinkhorn distance and establish its differentiability, a necessary condition
for end-to-end training. Building on this foundation, we demonstrate how our
model, DEPT, can be trained in a self-supervised manner by comparing the
distance between local image features across randomly chosen scales and
orientations. Furthermore, we prove the feature extractor's ability to
generalize across various orientations using the cross-Corr and cross-OT
metrics which are both invariant to orientation and show that it performs
competitively on popular benchmarks including linear baselines without the
need for additional data augmentation.

In various fields of study, a significant interest exists in the influence of local collaborations and networks on disease spread and vaccination effectiveness. To investigate this, a stochastic discrete transmission model of COVID-19 is developed for a population divided into public health districts, with each district conducting separate contact tracing. The model considers three levels of collaboration between these contact tracing units - none, partial, and complete - to analyze their individual contributions. By analyzing district-specific and global outcomes, it becomes evident that local collaborations significantly impact contact tracing efficiency, leading to enhanced findings in settings of partial collaboration and reduced findings in those of complete collaboration. Our work contributes a method for assessing contact tracing performance through contact tracing units and suggests the utilization of local collaborations in optimizing COVID-19 control and management policies.

Determining the fundamental parameters of open clusters is a complex undertaking that requires the combination of multiple astronomical observations and methods. Using the Gaia DR2 celestial survey, we aims to accurately establish the basic characteristics of Melotte 72. Melotte 72 is a rich star cluster located approximately 2300 parsecs from the Earth, in the constellation of Scorpius, and is believed to be around 1.0 billion years old. With the Gaia DR2 survey, the mass range of Melotte 72 can be defined by identifying eight sequence fitting methods and applying eight different starting points for a magnetic field, as well as utilizing the isochrone fitting technique with theoretical isochrones from MIST software and the 3Myr dummy star to calculate the cluster's physical parameters. Two methods of calculating distance were employed: one based on the cluster's reddening and color-magnitude diagram, and another from the cluster's membership stars and their spatial distribution. Additionally, we employed two methods of calculating cluster mass: one based on the cluster's radius and surface density, and another based on the cumulative mass of the cluster's astrotwins from the Gaia DR2 survey. These methods and calculations were repeated for various initial parameters and the minimum and optimum values were selected for each parameter based on consistency and plausibility. The optimum parameters found through our analysis include a distance of 2300 parsecs, mass of $7.4 \times10^4$ solar masses, radius

We examine the topological properties of paths with a total length below $n$, generated by independent Gaussian processes, where the functions defining these processes have a magnitude bounded by $\lambda$. Our results demonstrate that for large $n$, the expected Betti numbers for these paths have values similar to those found in a study by Bayer and Curto. However, this holds true only when the total length of these paths is the product of $n$ and $\lambda$, and when $\lambda > 1$. For $\lambda \leq 1$, the paths either have few or no non-trivial topological features. In a related context, the paths form a geometric object known as a Gaussian wandering, which was studied by Shiu. To calculate the Betti numbers, we first find the persistent homology images of these paths under a specific topological transformation, and then determine the expected values of these images by applying techniques from point process theory and making a four-fold symmetry assumption.

We've designed an algorithm that enables a robot arm to adjust its gripper camera by using just one image taken from an external camera. By leveraging advanced computer vision techniques, our system can construct 3D models of a room and calculate where fixtures, like screws or holes, are likely to be in the environment. It then makes adjustments to the gripper camera based on this predicted location, resulting in more accurate image calculations and enhanced object detection capabilities. By using this approach, our system can successfully find fixtures in real-time through just one image and also outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on a dataset of industrial images. Additionally, our system can accurately detect and locate objects in environments where there are no visible signs of fixtures and in cases where there are obstacles blocking the view.

From inverse reinforcement learning to constrained reinforcement learning, a new variant is explored, which implements the latter using the former. This paper demonstrates that all constrained MDPs with commutative and monoidal constraints can be represented as a single, targeted safety constraint at the expert level. Furthermore, it proves that expert-level IL can be utilized to enforce safety through the application of constraint projection. Notably, it shows that safety constraints specified at the expert level can be learned from suboptimal expert demonstrations. A method referred to as reverse constrained reinforcement learning is proposed, framework-agnostic and theoretically grounded, which can be used to train safe policies in constrained MDPs. A range of constraints, including those focused on action, state, and action-state pairs, as well as more complex group-based constraints, were successfully implemented in the experiment. Moreover, it shows that our approach to learning these complex constraints is just as effective as maximizing a mixture of the weights of the individual, basic constraints that collectively comprise it.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D map of the galaxy by tracking over 10,000,000 stars, which the mission's scientists believe will provide insight into the galaxy's structure, origin, and composition of dark matter. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the mission, its goals, and procedures, as well as the initial findings from the mission. According to the research, the galaxy consists of 13 billion to 20 billion stars within a radius of 26,000 light-years. The mission's scientists determined the mass of the galaxy to be approximately 8.3 million solar masses. The research also revealed that the galaxy rotates around an axis, but it challenges a long-held understanding of the galaxy's structure due to the unexpectedly high velocity of stars near the periphery. The findings from the mission may also indicate the presence of dark matter. According to the research, the galaxy's bulge consists of both ancient and intermediate-aged stars. The mission's scientists discovered several groups of stars with unique chemical properties, which were likely formed at different times. The research also confirmed that stars with higher masses burn through their fuel supplies more quickly, resulting in fewer appearances in the mission's data. Based on the mission's data, the research was also able to determine the galaxy's structure and motion within the surrounding space. The research was able to develop models for the galaxy's various components, which were then used to assess a subsequent space observatory's capabilities.

For computing minimum fill-in orderings with low treewidth, we examine the effect of starting with an initial vertex removal sequence. This sequence can be further improved by applying 'compact vertex dividers', which are derived from a limited number of tree-decompositions. Our experiments show that these dividers can enhance existing methods like Chordal Screwing Orderings and Plaxton-Rheinsteiner orderings, leading to reduced computational times and better outcomes in testing, especially with random graph generators.

Network analysis through inference and measurement has significant implications for understanding complex systems, particularly in life sciences, where the structure and function of various biological processes have been debated for centuries. The focus on these phenomena led to the consideration of weighted networks with capabilities beyond their binary form. However, existing literature still primarily deals with networks composed of doublets, neglecting the rich insights obtained from inferred and measured quadruplets. To address this knowledge gap, a comprehensive framework for weighted quadruplets is proposed to capture group relationships in a diverse setting of heterogeneous networks.

We suggest a method to validate physics-based neural networks through an authorized machine learning approach. This technique, called AML, provides a more reliable calculation of the potential error in a neural network's predictions. Unlike existing post-training error estimation methods, AML can learn intricate relationships between input variables and errors, given additional training on input-error pairs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AML for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by applying it to two problems: solving the Poisson equation and Elliott's phase-field model for two immiscible fluids. AML achieves accurate error assessments within a relatively small multiplier factor, often no more than 2, making it more suitable for practical use than previous methods. Additionally, AML has other benefits, such as the ability to perform cross-validation without an additional model, which can reduce computational costs. This paper is the first to apply AML to PINNs, expanding its applicability to problems that were previously difficult for post-training error estimation methods to solve.

Epidemiological research utilizes statistical analysis and mathematical modeling to study disease patterns. In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, various diseases have been characterized. We can examine the spread of the disease across specific geographical areas, such as cities, by applying statistical models, thereby enabling researchers to predict outcomes like infection and death rates. To accurately apply these models, practitioners must carefully collect and prepare the data, including precise spatial coordinates for better geographical visualization and understanding. We begin by reviewing the data collection process and provide a detailed explanation of handling this information along with examples. Furthermore, we examine the data pre-processing stage, analyzing datasets from Aragon's Covid19 project (https://github.com/Argo-covid19/ArGoC19) to illustrate best practices. We also discuss the importance of incorporating data from various sources, such as atmospheric models, to better understand the disease dynamics. In ArGoC19, there are time series data on local weather and atmospheric conditions, such as temperature, humidity, and air quality, along with data on the region's population density and mobility. By integrating this information, researchers can develop more accurate mathematical models that influence disease spread. In addition, using geostatistical methods with statistical software like R, R through snakepythons library, and Python through rsstools package, and machine learning algorithms can help predict the progression of the disease in a specified region.

To differentiate the zero-bias peak associated with Majorana edges from those caused by topological insulator edges or magnetic impurities, we suggest a tunneling spectroscopy technique involving ohmic contacts made with the electrode's high impedance characteristics in mind. Theoretical models indicate this method enables a specific ratio of Majorana peak height to the competing peaks to distinguish Majorana peaks, even when the latter's height is comparable to the former. Furthermore, this technique requires less stringent implications for the quality factor of the quantum dot than previously suggested. To implement this strategy, we recommend utilizing an ME core-based tunneling probe that produces high impedance, fabricated using a technology similar to that involved in the initial development of these devices. Theoretical models indicate this design could successfully differentiate Majorana peaks with a resolution of 50 millivolts per nanometer, given an assumed ohmic contact with 50 ohms per square micron. Theoretical models also suggest this technique would be effective in identifying Majorana peaks with other, similar tunneling spectroscopy approaches. However, this technique possesses an advantage in requiring minimal modification to the existing design and functionality of the tunneling probes.

To assess the performance of linear bandits, researchers typically rely on metrics such as regret bounds. The primary advantage of this measure is that it enables the analysis of algorithmic efficiencies in terms of a standard loss function across various action spaces. However, while useful for certain applications, regret bounds have several limitations when used as a standalone metric for evaluating loss functions applied in online learning contexts. In our investigation, which involves a broad class of action spaces called affine subspaces, we find that some well-established linear bandit algorithms may not provide effective solutions in diverse scenarios. In response, we also develop new solutions tailored to distinct action space configurations. In addition to these contributions, which are relevant to any online linear bandit setting, we take into account the specific requirements and constraints of an actionable recommendation model. In particular, we find that some of our newly designed algorithms may not be suitable for applications that involve cost-sensitive environments and probabilistic action selection. In response, we refine our approach to address these limitations and develop the first known affine action linear bandit algorithm capable of achieving sublinear regret bounds in diverse settings, even for cost-sensitive environments. Theoretical analyses and empirical evaluations of our findings are presented.

Graphene with gaps has been proposed to exhibit the valley Hall effect, but it's actually possible to demonstrate an orbital Hall effect under the same conditions. The application of a chiral optical beam can rotate the orbital magnetic moment of electrons, causing them to move in specific directions when an external magnetic field is present. This orbital Hall effect can be observed in uniformly curved, monolayer carbon nanosheets, and its consequences for electronic devices have significant implications.

Machine learning models' success is often compromised by data contamination, which can impair even the most advanced models. Graph neural networks excel at predicting node and graph properties but are vulnerable to data pollution, mainly due to their inherent structural dependencies. Current approaches mainly focus on removing structural data pollution by revising predictions according to graph convolutions. This paper proposes a novel reinforcement learning strategy to counter both structural and feature data pollution by revising predictions based on graph convolutions and feature modifications. Our experiments show that this method outperforms existing methods in predicting node and graph properties.

To improve multi-wavelength object identification between various astronomical surveys, researchers typically employ catalog matching methods. These techniques are crucial for correlating data across different surveys and are often used to create comprehensive astronomical catalogs. The key factors influencing the effectiveness and precision of catalog matching methods include survey astrometry and photometry. While photometric measurements are often available for most surveys, astrometric data can be unreliable or of low quality in some cases. To address this issue, a novel approach for catalog matching has been developed, leveraging photometric data from matched objects to refine astrometric data and increase the efficiency of catalog correlations. The performance and precision of this new method, dubbed PHOT-ALIGNMENT, have been evaluated using real-world astronomical data from the All-Sky Automated Survey for Source Identification and the Gaia-Gaia-Photometric Survey Atlas. By incorporating photometric data into the astrometric calibration process, PHOT-ALIGNMENT has demonstrated superior performance and precision, particularly for objects that express photometric parallax discrepancies. The results show that using photometric data in astrometric calibration significantly enhances, on average, the alignment of catalog objects, with a margin of at least 50% and up to 300% based on the specific conditions of the datasets used. Additionally, applying PHOT-ALIGNMENT to a pair of real-world astronomical datasets, comprising survey data from the All-Sky Automated Survey for Source Identification and the Gaia-Gaia-Photometric Survey Atlas, resulted

Covering a given hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ with a specific structure, like spheres of a certain radius, yet using edge covers that have fewer than $r$ edges each, is a critical issue. The simplest form of such coverage is called a minimal $r$-cover. Although it's well understood that minimal $r$-covers exist for $r$ and infinite $\mathcal{H}$, determining the exact edge count in these minimal $r$-covers poses a problem. For $r=2$, it's confirmed that the minimal edge count grows infinitely as the radius increases, a property held by all infinite $\mathcal{H}$ with a specific diameter. Our research has shown that for $r=2$, $\mathcal{H}$ with a specific diameter has a minimal edge count that grows infinitely as the radius increases. Moreover, for $r>2$, it's confirmed that the minimal edge count grows infinitely as $r$ increases. Furthermore, for $r$ and infinite $\mathcal{H}$ where the shortest edge length is $2$, it's confirmed that the minimal edge count grows infinitely as the radius increases.

Domain-specific vocabularies and concepts are frequently organized in more complex knowledge structures known as ontologies to ensure seamless communication between experts and non-experts. However, as ontologies expand, it becomes increasingly difficult for users to locate precise terminology or understand nuanced distinctions when searching for specific terms. To address this challenge, we propose OntoPlot, a novel visualization system that seamlessly integrates text search, hierarchical organization, and network analysis for in-depth ontology exploration. OntoPlot combines an intuitive graph view of ontologies with a hierarchically-organized list view and a dedicated text search panel, all seamlessly integrated to support multi-modal querying and network exploration. OntoPlot allows users to link search results to visual representations of the ontology and streamline navigation between related concepts. To further enhance user experience, we also developed sophisticated query suggestions based on ontology structure, contextual information, and historical user interactions. We showcased OntoPlot's capabilities by applying it to the search of biomedical knowledge, leveraging the extensive resources managed by the NCI Thesaurus, a comprehensive collection of biomedical terminology and concepts.

We have developed an innovative semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition framework that leverages unlabelled data for enhanced performance. Our approach involves two main components: a novel inter-domain loss introduced from the field of unsupervised domain adaptation, and a cycle-consistency loss derived from CycleGAN. The inter-domain loss empowers the model to make the most of its knowledge gained while training on labelled data, while the cycle-loss ensures that the speech-representative features extracted from both domains are in perfect sync. Notably, our semi-supervised framework outperforms its fully-supervised counterpart by as much as 4.5% in terms of word error rate, even when presented with labelled data of modest quantity. Thorough experiments and ablations reveal that the inter-domain loss plays a crucial role in enhancing performance on out-of-domain test sets.

In Bayesian active inference, an agent adjusts its predictive model of its environment based on its observations and desired actions. This framework has been found to facilitate successful navigation by robots. However, there are various approaches to integrating this method, each with its own complexities. This paper develops a simplified, efficient, and robust navigation system for a robot moving in two-dimensional space. It employs a predictive model with a Gaussian distribution, assuming that landmarks are generated by a prior Gaussian distribution. By taking into account only the variance of observations and the variance of landmark generation, the robot can efficiently update its beliefs. The robot can also determine the most effective observations and take purposeful actions towards its desired goals. Experimental results demonstrate that this simplified navigation system is successful in comparison to more complex approaches. It is also more computationally efficient, making it easier to implement on smaller robots.

The contribution of soft polymers' internal mobility to the Soret effect, observed in polymer blends under temperature gradients, has been mathematically derived and compared to experiments. The results indicate a substantial, non-negligible influence of internal freedom on this phenomenon. Theoretically obtained values align well with measured values in certain cases, while diverging in other instances. Possible reasons for these discrepancies with experimental data will also be explored.

The primary objective of music composition is to express emotions and connect with others through sound. This process is contrasted by the goal of music analysis, which seeks to understand underlying concepts and emotions. When applying artificial intelligence to music composition, the outcome often resembles random or childish patterns that lack emotional depth. This study argues that transforming composition, separating it from music notation, can facilitate more straightforward modeling and improve outcomes. Additionally, we argue that a pre-trained, large-scale language model is an efficient tool for learning composition-specific concepts and constraints without requiring predefined models. Our proposed method involves two primary steps: initial suggestions followed by iterative refinement. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by presenting a system that creates coherent musical stories and demonstrates its superiority over existing methods through a comparison of composition quality.

This study addresses the challenge of generating domain adaptation techniques that can reduce false positives in finding specific objects within images, focusing on pedestrian identification. A new method, called the box re-rank, was developed to discard false positive predictions made by classifiers. It works by re-evaluating the predictions in a shared space with an unrelated classification model. Initial results showed that our technique can effectively eliminate false positives on the CUHK-PEDES and Street-to-Signature datasets, significantly improving detection accuracy. Moreover, the technique can be combined with other domain adaptation methods to enhance its performance. It was found that our method can effectively adapt to domain differences. In addition, the technique can be used to mitigate the effects of false positives in general object detection tasks. It was tested on the MIND dataset and showed a substantial 8.1% improvement in detection accuracy. The source code of our technique has been made available online at https://github.com/huaylec/box-re-rank.

This paper utilizes a 2D Gaussian spectrum model to generate images based on impaired speech, and employs a neural network to restore these spectra, yielding improved quality. Since speech spectra are one-dimensional, a conventional solution involves first converting the images to 1D before inversion. Our research explores an alternative, where images are entirely represented by 1D spectral information, with only the background containing irrelevant information. This paradigm shifts the focus to identifying relevant content and discards the rest. Given the vast possibility of irrelevant information, a conventional CNN would struggle, so we propose an efficient neural network to separate relevant and irrelevant features. Our network successfully restores 1D spectra and delivers high-quality audio through a 64 vector speech synthesis model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a significant improvement in PESQ score from 1.05 to 1.56. Since our images only contain relevant features, they can be used in the future to improve speech recognition through multi-modal learning.

In this research, we examine the impact of an error in estimating the point where a throw begins on the overall movement of the arm. Unlike previous studies focusing on end-effectors like fingers, our study centers on throws, which are crucial in sports like baseball, golf, and discus throwing. Since throws involve a high degree of rotation and are largely controlled by the starting position, we developed a computational model to simulate how arm movements evolve over time. This model revealed that a single point of maximum extension differs significantly from the point of maximum extension when accurate throwing mechanics are applied, and we identified a method to transform one movement to the other while maintaining synchronization. Using a virtual reality interface with 6 degrees of freedom, we asked participants to both accurately and inaccurately throw a virtual ball, and our results demonstrated that targeting a specific point with the hand is difficult if the arm's extension point deviates from the throwing mechanics.

To incorporate syntax-based decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture is proposed, which uses a tree Structured Autoencoder to pre-learn syntax patterns from paired neural encoders and decoders. This approach enables Syntax-based Logging to occur after the source sentence has been translated, allowing for the selection of more accurate target trees and refined predictions. To optimize reordering, an order inference stage is introduced, using the pre-learned syntax to determine the best word order for translation, outperforming current decoding methods. Experiments on English-to-German and English-to-Russian datasets demonstrate the superiority of this method compared to standard NMT and syntax guided baselines.

Accurate calculations of molecular binding energies are vital in understanding various chemical processes related to astrochemistry by assessing the stability of molecules and their ability to release electrons or atoms and ions. In order to cover a broad range of molecules and binding types, a new approach called the Binding Energy Assessment Platform is introduced, basing its standards on experimental data and average binding energies derived from DFT computations. This platform provides a database with over 4000 calculated binding energies for 106 different compounds, spanning 4 distinct binding types. To evaluate its standards, a new method called the Average Platform Value was established and applied to different molecules and binding types. These studies showed that the platform's guidelines are consistent with average values of binding energies. This framework aims to facilitate and expand astrochemical simulations by offering refined binding energy data for molecules and small clusters, thus enhancing our understanding of chemical reactions and molecular structures in space.

A multiplicative stochastic process with a sample-dependent minimum limit is proposed, and its characteristics are thoroughly analyzed, showing its similarity to a multiplicative stochastic process with a fixed minimum limit. Furthermore, the strategy for managing risk in financial industries is explored using this stochastic process, demonstrating its potential applications.

Quantum systems offer the potential for significant, unambiguous advantage over their classical counterparts, particularly in tasks related to probability and multipartite entanglement. Quantum systems, whether physical or abstract, exist in a state that follows the laws of linear evolution through a series of controlled rotation (Circuits) driven by variable frequency generators (drivers), known as Hamiltonians. Generating random quantum states is an essential part of many quantum-based algorithms, often produced by applying a shallow set of controlled rotation (Circuits) from random angle generators (angles) on an empty system, known as Hadamard test-preparation. Since achieving true randomness is essential but difficult to obtain in classical systems, we focus on part-sampling a random state by implementing a short sequence of controlled rotation (Circuits) with random angle generators (angles) on an empty system, known as shallow-RND. Shallow-RND combines elements of two classic methods for creating multipartite entangled states, known as Haar-measure and random-unitary. By merging the advantages of these approaches in a single scheme, we prove it meets the requirements for true randomness. Our solution is further explored through successful testing across various depth dimensions using classic models of quantum-based algorithms, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness.

We are studying the reflection coefficient for combined space and time, $k(t,x) = e^{i\phi + ik_{x}x + k_{0}t}$, in the Davey-Stewartson II equations. The system of two-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equations is given by $k_{tt} - k_{xx} - k_{yy} = \pm k_{x}k_{tt}$. In the preface to 'The Unified Method of Solving theInverse Problems for the Two-Dimensional 3D Schrödinger Equation', by V.E. Zakharov, it is stated that the direct problem is solved using the method of stationary characteristics, and the inverse problem is connected with the question of $k_{+}$ spectral parameter behavior at small $k_{x}$. The main objective of the current work is to investigate the properties of $k_{-}$, a second $k$ spectral parameter, which corresponds to a different sign in the DSII equation, and to determine the behavior of the reflection coefficient, $|R|^{2}$. The performance of text categorization models can be compromised due to the presence of inconsistent or missing information in training datasets. Traditional text categorization techniques have often relied on straightforward text transformation methods, such as removing stop words, which have limited effectiveness in eliminating inconsistencies and specializing models for the data at hand. In contrast, neural network models can adapt to dataset patterns through dynamic feature extraction, but may still be vulnerable to inconsistencies, especially if the features they've isolated have little relevance to the categorization task. To address these challenges, we've developed an algorithm that modifies an existing trained neural network model, such as a Transformer, by selectively replacing or deleting its existing features. Since this algorithm operates on the model's parameters alone, it's compatible with any neural network architecture and can be applied to any text categorization task. Our experiments involving standard datasets from the ACM Conference on Document Recognition reveal that our method enables robust text categorization by isolating irrelevant features on various document classification tasks.

We introduce a straightforward knowledge graph, structured in a hierarchical manner, and formulate it using the existing concepts within Transformer architecture component frameworks. Our graph is precomputed and fixed, and its flexibility allows it to accommodate diverse problems by modifying the query layer only. In contrast, traditional graph-based methods utilize graph generation as part of their training process, which complicates understanding, training, and efficiency. Building on this idea, we implement a meta-learning algorithm that exploits the hierarchical graph structure and applies it to the Ryerson CDI dataset, yielding an effective and efficient results retrieval procedure. Furthermore, by meta-learning, our approach achieves success without requiring additional training and achieves comparable results with CDILeaf, a cutting-edge and complex model.

This study delves into the stability of data extraction and quantization in low-resource machine translation models with limited training data. We discovered that tiny models developed using data extraction tend to perform poorly when applied to other tasks, whereas models trained through quantization exhibit greater adaptability. Building on this finding, we introduced a novel method for cross-domain adaptation in models trained with exclusion, effectively allowing models to learn from data meant for competitor approaches. This breakthrough enables the development of a lightweight MT model capable of achieving state-of-the-art results in sign language to Italian translation without requiring extensive sign language data.

We define a hypergraph as hypergraph G = (V, H> of a set of points, where the connections are described by a set of rules (H>, such that the rules dictate how the points interact. In a system, the interactions between the points are governed by a set of rules that vary with location, not uniformity, within the network. We identify the term "uniform graph" as being equivalent to a graph that has a single set of rules across its entire space, {H=phi}. Next, we explore the potential of a mathematical framework, Toeplovian theory, as a means to describe the behavior of a graph that becomes more complex over time, particularly those that involve multiple relationships. We demonstrate a fundamental property that applies to graphs uniformly, phi in H, yet does not necessarily apply to the more complex hypergraphs, especially those that are illogical and difficult to describe through traditional terms. Therefore, the term "uniform graph" holds significant value as a basic concept that distinguishes a simple from a complex system, particularly one that is illogical.

In medical image analysis, specifically for visual tasks like segmenting the lungs, a significant amount of ground truth data is traditionally required. This necessity drives a wide adoption of data augmentation techniques in the field. Contrary to the common belief that extensive ground truth data is necessary, we demonstrate in this research that accurate lung segmentation can be achieved with fewer labeled data, facilitated by our image processing module that refines the input images. This module is based on a U-Net architecture trained on relatively basic tasks such as combining multiple images and removing background noises. By integrating it into the traditional pipeline that includes training on augmented data and using a semantic segmentation approach, we significantly decrease the necessity for extensive ground truth data. This claim is substantiated through our experiments on Pneumonia dataset from the ISIC 2020 challenge. This technique not only reduces the data requirement but also proves cost-effective, translatable to other image analysis tasks, and operates without altering the base model, thereby ensuring maximum utilization of base model capabilities. To the best of our knowledge, this research is the first to utilize image processing techniques to diminish data labeling requirements in medical image analysis tasks. Additionally, we also release the source code of our research for the community to reference at https://github.com/mindr-lab/isp_u_net.

While fine-tuning large language models on image description generates excellent results, it requires significant computational resources and can be challenging due to unstable convergence issues. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a new approach using prompt tuning, which enables the model to adjust image description styles without readjusting the underlying image features. Additionally, this method develops a novel filter mechanism that allows for explicit control over the description style without compromising its image coherence. To further improve convergence stability, the paper incorporates an innovative technique using average within-model hyperstage ensembles to produce consistent results. This approach also gains an extra layer of adaptability due to pre-training the model on a large dataset with multiple perspectives. Both the prompt and hyperensemble strategies outperform the current state-of-the-art approach in description quality, according to Blue4 dataset evaluation, and also outperform previous bi-directional image description methods.

This research explores the concept of damage in advanced robot systems, examining how it affects prediction accuracy and overall performance. Current modeling approaches, whether simplified or complex, inherently incorporate damage elements due to their reliance on physical characteristics. However, existing algorithms tend to treat damage as a random element without considering its causal connections, which may lead to overestimations of uncertainty and neglect of potential performance degradation resulting from damage. A novel predictive model for random damage in structures has been developed, taking into consideration the role of corrosion and initial stress. By causal analysis, this research identifies corrosion as a primary risk factor for damage in areas with poor water access and to investigate further other potential sources. A robot performance model is introduced, examining how prediction error and damage interact. Simulation data collected from a hydraulic press test, combined with real-world damage reports on robots, are analyzed to test the newly developed approaches. These findings emphasize the need for advanced probabilistic models that capture the causal relationships between damage causes and robot performance.

The selection of a suitable neural network architecture is a crucial stage in any machine learning project, yet, even with expert guidance, there's no guarantee of its success. That's because different tasks require varying levels of complexity in their data representations - some necessitating simple, expandable systems while others need more intricate ones. This paper's focus is on 'growable' neural networks that dynamically adapt to increasing task demands by strategically integrating new computation modules, minimizing the need for expert-driven architecture selection. Our approach builds upon previous research in transform-based architectures and specializes in handling tabular data efficiently. We present a new deep learning framework called 'PicoAndGiant,' comprising a scalable and adaptable architecture component and a trainable backend, specifically designed to expand its capabilities as needed. PicoAndGiant incorporates MMLSpark's capabilities for seamless integration with Spark. Extensive experiments with this framework on public datasets at UfoRocketResearch.com demonstrate superior performance compared to established baseline models, outshining even state-of-the-art tabular data analyses while successfully scaling on large distributed computing environments.

Voice-based translations without additional voice output languages can be performed by adapting existing visual speech-substitition models to the challenge of zero-shot voice translation, which doesn't require audio inputs. We found that using a pre-trained encoder-only model for this purpose is viable, eliminating the need for complicated models or fine-tuning processes. We have set up a new dataset called the many-to-many zero-shot voice translation dataset, which allows for a diverse range of language combinations in both the input and output. We have conducted a initial study on this process and made it available so other researchers can continue exploring the topic.

This research focuses on non-incremental theories for general balance laws, with a special emphasis on modeling physical systems with boundary interactions that change over time. It builds upon previous work by Coleman and Gurtin in a similar context to investigate model equations that can describe both internal and boundary processes. These processes are represented by vector fields associated with boundary layers and internal regions respectively, both of which are part of a broader model equation that governs the system's behavior. This system's behavior is determined by an evolution rule for the associated fields, which is based on the concept of supply and energy dissipation. This framework enables the modeling of systems like fluids in contact with changing solid surfaces or with surface reactions that involve complex interfaces. Furthermore, this study shows that the model equations derived from this method are well-defined even when the system's boundaries change rapidly, are non-Lipschitz, and are influenced by various physical factors. This achievement is validated by examples of models for heat transfer, balance laws for mass and species transfer, and first-order chemical reactions. Moreover, this study shows that the model equations are consistent across different mathematical paradigms, which is illustrated by a model example. Finally, this study explores some challenges and obstacles that need to be addressed in future research, which will lead to more advanced mathematical models and applications.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy demand within the low voltage network (LVT) are vital for informing distribution system operators (DSOs) about upcoming distribution system conditions. These predictions enable the informed execution of flexible system management (FSM) strategies, including existing measures like load shedding and demand response. Although several forecasting methods are available to predict energy demand within the LVT, they often lack the required level of accuracy. This study investigates the utilization of load prediction models derived from historical data as well as probabilistic machine learning (ML) forecasting methods for LVT analysis. It focuses on the implementation of two advanced ML-based forecasting approaches for short-term demand prediction within the LVT, namely the filter forecaster and the forecast selector. These methods involve multiple base forecasters that generate initial predictions, which are then filtered and selected to form an ensemble forecast. The selection process is based on the utilization of hourly peak load characteristics, allowing the model to adjust the prediction accuracy based on the forecast horizon and seasonal variations of the peak load profile. The model's efficacy is evaluated using actual energy consumption data from over 4,500 Dutch LVTs. The outcomes indicate a considerable underprediction by traditional methods during summer, particularly for daily peak demand. In contrast, the proposed model demonstrates robust performance across various scenarios, showing reduced underprediction errors of up to 11% compared to traditional methods. While deep learning has achieved remarkable success in natural language processing and other areas, its applications in these domains require explicit integration of domain expertise. This integration, known as knowledge-rich learning, involves incorporating domain-specific knowledge into machine learning. A general framework for incorporating domain knowledge into deep models is presented, along with a method to stack neural learning layers with structured symbolic representations. An empirical demonstration of this framework is provided through a task that requires integrating domain-specific knowledge into a language model. The approach is applied to the TACSB dataset, and experimental results show that incorporating domain knowledge, encoded using formal methods in this case, can improve the accuracy of sequential binary predictions by up to 40 percent.

The significant impact of the COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in extensive research aimed at mitigating its effects. In medical community circles, researchers have been motivated to leverage data-driven approaches for diagnosing, treating, and preventing COVID-19. Relying solely on clinical images, without pathology annotation, is a common research strategy in epidemiology. However, due to the time-consuming nature of manual annotation, generating labeled data for machine learning is a complex task. There has been some research attempting to localize and segment COVID-19 lung lesions in chest CT scans without explicit labeling, either through weakly supervised learning methods or by using alternative modalities such as blood samples. Current learning approaches often require lesion mask annotations or pair histology and CT scans to identify patterns. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel deep learning framework that can automatically detect COVID-19 lesions from unlabelled scanning data. Our "unprejudiced learning" framework enables the model to detect lesions and predict lesion maps based on patch-level analysis. Our experiments show that the proposed model can effectively detect COVID-19 lesions and outperform existing lesion-level COVID-19 detection methods, with a performance that approaches that of segmentation models requiring full annotation. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

A crucial step in spinal radiology and bone density analysis in computer-aided diagnosis is vertebral body identification. Due to the repetitive nature of the spine, sophisticated techniques from image processing are required to accurately and precisely identify the vertebrae. From the initial problem of vertebral localization to the final identification of individual vertebrae, a new fully automated method addresses the entire process. The method involves a novel spine-rectification algorithm in the chest region followed by an optimization technique with reference points from image interpretation to localize the vertebrae correctly in 3D. The method successfully passes the majority of vertebrae through a reconstruction pipeline during image segmentation without needing user input in a quantifiable and accurate manner.

The ultrastrong coupling of light to matter has sparked new and innovative ideas within quantum electrodynamics research. Specifically,scattering electron processes have shown promise in this context,with the predicted effects potentially surpassing conventional formulas derived from perturbation theory. By numerically solving the Schrödinger equation,we have revisited these processes and found that an electron cavity system can stabilize through vacuum fluctuations when ultrastrong coupling is present. This stabilization outcome is a unique phenomenon that has not been seen before in quantum electrodynamics experiments.

In the last few years, a model called the Ground Interaction Model has been developed in the robotics field. This model separates the interactions between robots and the ground into three distinct processes: penetration, vibration and slipping. However, a major limitation of this model is its assumption that vibration and penetration can be treated as independent events that do not affect each other. Furthermore, it assumes that vibration and slipping can be treated as separate events with vibration not influencing slipping and vice versa. However, in many cases, these three processes are interlinked. To overcome this limitation, a new multi-physics Ground Interaction Model is developed, taking into account the dynamics of elastic actuators that are becoming more popular in robot design. The model is tested in a quadruped robot that is equipped with elastic actuators, specifically in its actuator springs and the legs' compliance characteristics. It is shown that both vibration and penetration can be utilized as well as reduced by the multi-physics model to optimize movement and reduce the workload. Additionally, some previous findings related to elastic actuation are confirmed through the multi-physics model. It is also shown that both vibration and penetration can be utilized as well as reduced by the multi-physics model to optimize movement and reduce the workload. The multi-physics model is utilized to analyze various quadruped gaits with elastic actuation, revealing that there are certain circumstances in which vibration and penetration can coexist and also reducing slipping can occur without penetration.

The quantum fundamental change stems from, at its core, a fundamental change in the ability to differentiate. That is to say, geometric analysis, born from Leibniz's infinitesimal calculus, finds its quantum counterpart in the infinitesimally small changes principle, where the non-commutativity of operators reflects the unique character of quantum differentiation that contrasts with classical differentiation. That is why solving the problem of differentiating a quantum function $F(\mathbf{r}, t)$ with respect to position $\mathbf{r}$ and time $t$ in a quantum system is essential for quantitatively understanding a quantum system is crucial. That being the case, we'll start by examining the eigenvalue equation for the position operator, then derive a way to differentiate a quantum function, which not only agrees with the known results but also offers a new way to understand the changes that occur in a quantum system, which also applies to understanding changes in almost any quantum observable. That understanding of quantum differentiation allows us to gain insight into how it applies to understanding changes in the Wigner function that describe an epistemic state of a quantum system. That being the case, we'll demonstrate that our approach to differentiating the Wigner function yields the correct Busch algorithm that describes quantum nonlocality that defines quantum fundamentals.

Theoretical and numerical studies of a local tear in a plasma slab have shown that a small change in its magnetic field can trigger rapid growth, exceeding 10 per unit length per 4Nth time unit, when the number of units is in the millions. This phenomenon occurs when electron temperatures become highly non-uniform, leading to a specific kinetic effect. Initially, growth is dominated by a specific particle fluid equation but eventually the particles' kinetic energy plays a dominant role. A scale-based model for this tear has been developed and tested. It predicts that the tear will only occur within a specific range of non-uniform temperatures, which may be influenced by factors not considered in this study. A possible connection between this tear and solar atmospheric phenomena has been suggested, which requires further observation and experimentation to confirm.

Recent advancements in fashion retrieval research have been attributed to improved image search techniques and the proliferation of fashion-related online data. Research has shifted from basic image-based matching to more sophisticated tasks, which require analyzing semantic connections between images and human preferences. Fashion designers aim to please consumers by combining style with meaning. Analysts in the field attempt to uncover correlations between image content and consumer tastes by identifying common patterns in fashion images. To address this goal, researchers have developed new methods for extracting key features from fashion images, which can manipulate attributes like gender and measure to create new outfit combinations from original images. Our study leverages a large dataset of Zalando's fashion catalog to compare various approaches to extracting key features. Our method, which uses a semi-supervised approach to align our manipulation targets with the actual image content, outperforms the best existing approach.

The convergence of dual gradient systems in Repellor dynamics is studied for recovering original data within a range of Banach spaces that incorporate norms with features of lasso and total variation. It's found that repulsive dynamics of dual systems yield consistent reconstruction under the Helinger-Fisz loss function, also achieving sparsity with certain norm choices. A novel application of dual gradient systems is presented for recovery of functions within Sobolev and Hardy spaces using the Helinger-Fisz function, as well as for quasi-isometric mapping of image data from unknown sources.

Capturing a complete light field with a central camera array is an intricate task, mainly due to the presence of occlusions that hinder obtaining a dense sampling of light field data. Current solutions typically rely on supplementary information, such as monocular or stereo data, to infer depth in the occluded regions of the light field. In this research, a new method is proposed to derive depth from the captured light field data without any additional information, addressing the occlusions in the process. The approach involves an adaptive process that dense samples the light field data, specifically targeting the occluded areas, using a cost function that simulates the appearance of the hidden objects. The results of the method are then used to calculate the light field depth through epipolar plane intersection, which yields the substantial outcome of the first benchmark of its kind to focus on depth estimation with occlusions, showcasing the proposed method's superiority over baseline approaches.

This study presents a new approach for solving the Fokas-Lenells equation, an extension of the nonlinear Schrodinger equation with rational, real, and purely imaginary coefficients. By applying the Fokas-Lenells formulas derived from the bilinear form of the equation, we resolve a long-standing uncertainty in the Fokas-Lenells direct approach, namely the origin of the two-layer (smooth and singular) initial conditions' system. We utilize the properties of the J-function from the bilinear form and the properties of the two-layer system to derive the Fokas-Lenells formulas, thereby offering a novel method for tackling Fokas-Lenells initial values that have previously proven intractable.

The effective action for non-uniform gravitational background fields derived from Double Field Theory is constructed and its Lagrangian form is determined. It serves as a validation for the proposal made by Tseytlin and Pacheco in 2008. The action of the theory, when applied to a metric deviating from the standard symplectic frame, yields an Euler-Lagrange equation solution that matches the equation for an extrinsic curvature term in a Ricci scalar based theory. The application of this solution demonstrates that Euler-Lagrange variational calculations for an action with an Euler-Lagrange form can lead to the same gravitational equation as variational calculations for an action with a Euler-Lagrange form based on an Euler-Lagrangian. To meet the demands of modern home networks, we're seeing an increase in the use of mesh networks. These networks, which allow multiple access points to communicate with each other, have several benefits including reduced dead spots and improved network coverage. However, the additional access points also create new sources of interference, which can negatively impact transmission speed and quality. By leveraging the capabilities of the IEEE 802.11k and v standards, it's possible to identify the most suitable location for an additional access point to be introduced into the network and ensure that it operates at its most efficient speed. Both mesh and non-mesh networks can benefit from these standards. In a mesh network, the standards can help balance the network load by moving traffic and adjusting operating speeds of mesh access points. In a non-mesh network, the standards can be used to identify which access points are overloaded and in need of support from an additional extender, which would then be configured automatically using the configuration methods specified in the IEEE 802.11v standard.
